notes.title: 1 · What's the catch?
notes.body:
They say: *"Okay, what's the catch?"*

> "No catch. It's built, it's real, and looking at it costs you nothing. If you want it live, the build runs seven forty-nine to fifteen forty-nine depending on size and how much automation goes behind it, plus a monthly for hosting and keeping it running. If you don't want it, then we built a website for nothing. Happens more than you'd think."

## Why it works

This is now your most common objection, and it is a good sign — a person asking about the catch is a person who is interested.

Answer it flat and fast. Any hedging here reads as a catch.

The last sentence is the one that does the work, so do not cut it.

notes.title: 2 · What does it cost?
notes.body:
They say: *"What am I looking at for something like that?"*

> "Fair question. The build runs somewhere between seven forty-nine and fifteen forty-nine, depending on how big it is and how much automation you want behind it."
>
> "There's a monthly on top for hosting and keeping it running, but Logan sets that off what you actually need — I'd be guessing, and I'd rather not guess at your money. Same with the CRM side if you ever wanted it, that's priced per person. That's a big part of what the ten minutes is for."

## Why it works

Give the range immediately and without hedging. It screens out anyone who was never going to spend it, and it stops them feeling like you dodged.

Then stop talking about money.

! **Never invent a monthly figure.** Logan sets it off what they actually need.
! **Never price the CRM or the automation packages.** Those are per person and they are Logan's call.
! **Never discount and never hint at flexibility** — including when they are about to say yes. You have no authority to move any of it and everyone on the call knows it.

If they say it is too much, that is a fit problem, not a price problem, and Logan will handle it.

notes.title: 3 · I already have a website
notes.body:
They say: *"I've already got one."*

> "Sure — and that's kind of the point. You can put them side by side and just see. Ten minutes, and if yours is better, keep yours."

## Why it works

The demo does this work for you, which is the whole point. You are not arguing about whether theirs is good, you are offering a comparison.

! **Never criticise their current site.**

## The one real disqualify

If they tell you they paid someone for it in the last year, that is a genuine disqualify.

Thank them, ask who built it, note the name, and get off the phone cleanly. Selling over fresh money is how you get a reputation in a small market.

notes.title: 4 · Just text me the link
notes.body:
They say: *"Just send it over and I'll take a look."*

> "Yeah, absolutely — what's the best number to send it to?"

Say yes instantly and never hedge. Text Logan the business name and it goes out the same day.

## Then take one swing at booking them today

> "And here's the thing — the next call is where we actually go through discovery. What you want it doing, what you want that phone ringing for. That's the part that makes it yours instead of just a page with your name on it. If I can get you booked this afternoon we can get this taken care of ASAP instead of dragging it out over two weeks."

A link with nobody on the other end converts badly. They open it for eight seconds while doing something else and it dies.

## If they still will not book

> "No problem at all. Let me get Logan and Garrett to take it from here — they'll get it over to you and follow up directly."

Hand it off and stop working it. Log it **SO** and text Logan and Garrett the name, number and email the same day.

It is not your call to chase from there, and letting go of it cleanly is worth more than a second attempt.

! **Do not send the link yourself.** Text Logan the business name and he sends it, so what lands in their inbox is the version he wants them looking at.

notes.title: 5 · Not interested
notes.body:
They say: *"Not interested, thanks."*

> "Totally fair — I called you out of nowhere. Only thing I'd say is it's already built, so there's nothing to get out of. If you ever want to see it, I'm [Your Name] at ProyTech. Take care."

## Why it works

One attempt, said lightly, then let them go.

If they say no twice, thank them and hang up — genuinely. A setter who pushes past a second no costs us far more in a market this size than the deal was worth.

Log it and move to the next number.

notes.title: Things you cannot say
notes.body:
Check this when you are unsure mid-call. It is a reference, not something you read start to finish.

! **No results promises.** Traffic, leads, calls, rankings, "you'll be number one on Google," "guaranteed." None of it, not even as a joke. Search promises in particular are how agencies get sued.
! **No timelines.** No launch date either. You do not know, and being wrong creates a problem Logan has to clean up on a live call.
! **No price outside the build range.** Seven forty-nine to fifteen forty-nine and nothing else. Never a monthly figure, never a CRM or automation price, never a discount, never "I might be able to do something" — including when they are about to say yes.
! **No client names.** "A top-ten agent here in Wichita" is fine. The name is not yours to give out.
! **Never say it is free.** Not a gift, not giving it away. Looking is free. The site is not.
! **Never send the link yourself.** Text Logan the business name and he sends it — that way what lands in their inbox is the version he wants them looking at.
! **Nothing about how it is built.** What it runs on, which vendors are involved — "that's Logan's side of the house" covers all of it.
! **No one else's numbers.** Another business's volume or pricing, including a client's. Wichita is small and it gets back around.
! **Never imply you are an employee.** You are an independent representative. If asked directly, say exactly that.

notes.title: 0. How this call works
notes.body:
You are not selling a website. You are telling someone a website already exists with their name on it, and asking if they will spend ten minutes looking at it.

That is a much easier sentence to say and a much easier sentence to hear — and it is the only thing on this call that is genuinely unusual to the person picking up.

## The job

- **One job: ten minutes on Logan's calendar.** You never demo it yourself, you never quote past the website price, you never negotiate.
- **Expect roughly thirteen dials per booked call.** The twelve nos are the cost of the thirteenth. That is the math working, not you failing.
- **"I don't know — Logan will" is a professional answer.** It has never lost anyone a deal. Guessing has.
- **If they ask to see it right there on the phone, the answer is yes.** Text Logan the business name and he will have it up in minutes. Never stall on that question — it is the most interested a prospect ever gets.

## What you may say about money

You may give the build range: seven forty-nine to fifteen forty-nine, depending on size and how much automation sits behind it.

! **Never put a number on the monthly.** That is quoted per client.
! **Never price the CRM or the automation packages.** Those are per person, and they are Logan's call.

notes.title: 1. The opener
notes.body:
> "Hey — is this [First Name]? … [First Name], this is [Your Name] over at ProyTech, here in Wichita. This is going to be a slightly odd call. Can I have thirty seconds?"

## Then stop talking

Let them say "sure."

The pause is what makes the rest feel like a conversation instead of a pitch.

notes.title: 2. The in
notes.body:
> "So — we build websites for [see the swap table] around here. And rather than call and pitch you on it, we went ahead and built one for [Company Name]. No obligation, nothing to sign, I'm not asking you to buy anything today. I just want to get it in front of you and let you look at it. Takes ten minutes."

## Why it works

Say "no obligation" once and mean it. Do not repeat it three times — repeating it is what makes people think there is one.

Say it like it is already done, because it is.

! **Do not soften it into "we could build you one."** That is a different call and a much weaker one.

notes.title: 3. Why would you do that?
notes.body:
They say: *"Wait — you built me a website? Why would you do that?"*

> "Honestly? Because telling people about it doesn't work. Everybody's had somebody call them about a website. It's faster to just build the thing and let you look at it. If you like it, we'll talk. If you don't, you're out ten minutes and I'll leave you alone."

## Why it works

This is the most important answer in the whole script, because it is completely true and they can hear that it is.

Do not dress it up. Do not add a benefit. Say it and stop.

notes.title: 4. Six industries — swap these words
notes.body:
Everything else stays the same. Only these four things change based on who picked up.

| Who you called | Say we build for | The line that lands | Hand to Logan + Garrett if |
|---|---|---|---|
| Real estate agent | agents around here | "…answers the person who fills out a form while you're in a showing." | Team lead, 25+ deals, or owns the brokerage |
| Lender | loan officers around here | "…catches the application that comes in at nine at night." | Runs a branch or has LOs under them |
| Roofing | roofers around here | "…answers the call you miss when you're on a roof." | More than two crews, or already running ads |
| HVAC / plumbing | HVAC companies around here | "…books the service call while you're under a house." | More than three trucks, or a dispatcher |
| Auto / PDR | shops around here | "…answers the estimate request while you're on a car." | Multiple bays or more than one location |
| Landscaping | landscaping companies around here | "…catches the quote request while you're on a mower." | Year-round crews, or commercial accounts |

## Using the line that lands

It goes in whenever they ask what makes it different, or when the call needs a nudge. It is specific to their day, which is why it works.

Use it once — it is a line, not a theme.

notes.title: 5. Which call you are booking
notes.body:
There are two kinds of prospect on the other end of this and they get booked differently. You need one question to tell them apart, and it sounds like small talk.

> "Before I take up more of your time — how big is the operation these days? Is it mostly you, or do you have people?"

## Small operator — the usual case

Book the ten minutes with Logan to walk through the demo. This is the standard path and most of your calls.

## Bigger operation

See the last column of the swap table for what counts as bigger.

> "Got it — then honestly the website's the small piece for someone your size. Let me get you thirty minutes with Logan and Garrett instead. They'll show you the site, but they'll also show you what runs behind it for an outfit with [crews / a team / multiple locations]. That's a better use of your time than me talking."

Log it **HV** and text Logan the same day. Do not let it sit overnight.

! **Do not pitch the site as the whole thing to a bigger operation, and do not talk price at all.**

notes.title: 6. Book it
notes.body:
> "Are mornings or afternoons better for you?"

They pick. Then narrow immediately — never offer an open calendar.

> "Perfect. Thursday at ten, or Thursday at two?"

## Do not hang up without all of these

A booked call with a missing mobile number is a no-show.

- Full name, spelled back to them
- Best email — read it back
- Best mobile — read it back

## Confirm the invite

> "You'll get a calendar invite from Logan in the next few minutes. If it's not there in ten, check spam and text me."

## Set the frame

> "He'll have yours up on the screen when you get on. Ten minutes, and there's nothing on the other side of it."

notes.title: 7. Five things to grab before you hang up
notes.body:
Logan tightens their site up in the half hour before the appointment, so what they see is about their business and not a generic version of it. He can only do that if you got these on the call.

Ninety seconds, and it is the difference between a good demo and a great one. Ask it like you are being thorough, because you are.

1. The business name exactly how they want it written
2. Their current website, if they have one
3. The three things they actually want more of — *"if you could pick what the phone rings for, what is it?"*
4. Where they work — town, radius, or the areas they cover
5. Where their photos live: *"Facebook? Google? He'll pull from there unless you'd rather send some over."*

## Why the last one matters

That question does double duty. It gets Logan what he needs, and it makes the whole thing feel real to them before they ever get on the call — which is most of why people actually show up.

notes.title: 8. Voicemail
notes.body:
> "[First Name], it's [Your Name] with ProyTech here in Wichita. Odd reason for the call — we built a website for [Company] and I wanted to see if you'd take a look at it. Nothing to sign. [Number]. Again, [Number]. Thanks."

## The rules

- **First attempt only.** Never on the second or third — that turns you into a telemarketer in their contacts.
- Under fifteen seconds.
- Say the number twice, slowly.

notes.title: SOP-01 · Running a calling block
notes.body:
How a productive call day goes, and what the numbers should look like while you are learning.

## The numbers, honestly

Logan books **one appointment per thirteen dials**. He has been doing this a while and it is a genuinely good rate.

Expect **one per twenty-five to thirty in your first two weeks**, improving toward **one per fifteen to eighteen by week four**.

Your first ten days will produce almost nothing. That is not a warning, it is the normal shape of this. Nobody is drawing conclusions about you in week one.

## Before the block — fifteen minutes

- List is loaded and sorted before you dial the first number. Never start a block by building a list — it kills the hour.
- Script and the qualification questions in front of you. Not open in a tab. In front of you.
- Water, phone charged, door shut, notifications off.

## The block itself

- **Dial in sets of twenty with no stopping.** Momentum is most of this — the fourth call is always better than the first.
- **Log the disposition code the second you hang up.** Five seconds. The full note goes in between sets.
- Five minutes between sets. Stand up, walk somewhere, do not check your phone.
- Two sets is a block — roughly sixty to ninety minutes. Two blocks is a full calling day.
- **Never dial the same number twice inside one block.**

## When people actually pick up

- **Service businesses** — roofing, HVAC, auto, landscaping: 8 to 10am and 4 to 6pm. Midday they are on jobs.
- **Agents and lenders**: 9 to 11am and 1 to 3pm. Avoid weekends — they are showing.

This is what has worked, not a schedule you are being handed. If you find better hours, take them and tell Logan so we can use it.

## Ending the block

1. Every row logged and complete. No blanks, no "will fill in later."
2. Every booking texted to Logan — see SOP-03.
3. Anything marked **HV** or **SO** handed to Logan and Garrett the same day.
4. One line to Logan: dials, conversations, bookings. Takes ten seconds and it is how we spot a problem in week two instead of week five.

notes.title: SOP-02 · Logging and dispositions
notes.body:
Every dial gets a row before the next dial. This is the part that looks like admin and is actually the whole thing.

## Why this one matters more than it looks

At day fourteen we sit down and decide whether this is working.

If the log is honest, we can tell whether the problem is the list, the opener, or the offer — and fix the right one. If the log is thin or flattering, we cannot tell anything, and the conversation becomes about you instead of about the process.

Log the bad calls exactly as carefully as the good ones.

## The nine codes

| Code | Means | What has to be true |
|---|---|---|
| **NA** | No answer | Rang out. No voicemail left. Attempt count goes up by one. |
| **BAD** | Bad number | Dead, wrong or disconnected. The number never works. It does **not** use up an attempt — the lead dies on the spot. |
| **VM** | Voicemail left | First attempt only. Never leave a second one. |
| **CB** | Callback | They gave you a specific day and time. Write the exact time, not "next week." |
| **NF** | Not a fit | Disqualified on the call. The reason goes in the row — no blank reasons. |
| **SO** | Send only | Wanted the link, would not book. Handed to Logan and Garrett the same day. |
| **BK** | Booked | Time agreed, contact details captured, Logan texted. |
| **HV** | High value | Bigger operation. Handed to Logan and Garrett, never worked yourself. |
| **DNC** | Do not call | They asked not to be contacted. Permanent. Tell Logan the same day. |

## What goes in the row

- Date · business name · contact name · phone · industry
- Disposition code
- **Their words** — what they said to the hook question, quoted, not summarised. "We just let it go to voicemail" is useful. "Not great at follow-up" is not.
- Any objection you hit, and what you said back — including the ones you handled. Especially those.
- Next action and the date it happens

## Three rules

1. **Write their words, not your read on them.** Your read changes; the quote does not.
2. **NF always carries a reason.** A disqualify with no reason is a lost lead dressed up as a decision.
3. **DNC is permanent and immediate.** No follow-up, no "one more try in a month," no exceptions. Tell Logan the same day.

If you catch yourself not wanting to log a call, that is the one worth logging. Nobody has ever been in trouble here for a bad call. Being unable to explain a bad week is a different problem.

notes.title: SOP-03 · Booking and handoff
notes.body:
The ninety seconds after they say yes. Get this wrong and the appointment does not happen.

## On the call, in this order

1. **Lock the time.** "Thursday at ten, or Thursday at two?" Never offer an open calendar.
2. **The five things Logan needs to build it:** business name exactly as they want it written · their current website if they have one · the three things they want the phone ringing for · where they work, town or radius · where their photos live.
3. **Full name, spelled back. Email, read back. Mobile, read back.** All three, every time.
4. **Confirm the invite.** "You will get a calendar invite from Logan in the next few minutes. If it is not there in ten, check spam and text me."
5. **Set the frame.** "He will have yours up on the screen when you get on. Ten minutes, and there is nothing on the other side of it."

## Within ten minutes of hanging up

Text Logan, in one message: business name · contact name · phone · email · the time booked · industry · the five things. Then log it **BK**.

Ten minutes is not a formality. Logan builds their site in the half hour before the appointment — he cannot start until your text lands, and an appointment he finds out about an hour late is an appointment he walks into cold.

## No-shows

- Send one text within fifteen minutes: "Hey [Name] — Logan is on and ready when you are, everything alright?"
- If nothing, one attempt to rebook later that day or the next.
- If they no-show twice, log **NF** and move on. Do not chase a second no-show — it is the clearest answer you will get.

## Reschedules and cancellations

- A reschedule is yours to fix. Same-day text, new time, re-confirm, re-text Logan.
- A cancellation gets one question: "Just timing, or is it not for you?" Timing goes to **CB** with a date. Anything else goes to **NF** with the reason.

notes.title: SOP-04 · Follow-up, callbacks and send-only
notes.body:
Most reps lose their week here — chasing people who already answered them.

## Send only (SO)

They wanted the link and would not book. Take one swing at booking them the same day using the discovery line in the script. If they still will not, hand it over and stop.

- Text Logan and Garrett the same day: name, business, number, email.
- Log it **SO**. It leaves your list at that point.

This is not you giving up. It is a lead that needs a different conversation than the one you are equipped to have, and it is worth more to us in Logan and Garrett's hands than sitting in your follow-up pile for three weeks.

## Callbacks (CB)

- Call at the **exact time** they gave you. Not the same day, the time.
- Open differently: "Hey [Name] — you asked me to try you back this afternoon." That is a warm call now. Do not re-run the cold opener.
- If they blow off two agreed callback times, it is an **NF**. They have answered you.

## Not a fit (NF)

- Dead, unless the reason was timing. If it was timing, set a real date and let it go until then.
- Never re-work an NF because you had a slow week. That is how a list gets burned.

## The attempt cap

- **Three attempts on a cold number across two weeks, then it dies.** Voicemail on the first attempt only.
- **A bad number does not get three attempts.** Log **BAD** the first time you hear it is dead, wrong or disconnected, and the lead stops there. Spending the other two dials on a number that will never work is two dials gone.
- Four or more calls to someone who has never picked up is not persistence, it is how we end up on a DNC list.

## Do not call

! **DNC is immediate, permanent and has no exceptions.** Never a "well, they were just having a bad day."

Log **DNC**, tell Logan the same day, and it never gets dialled again. This one is not a judgement call and there is no version of it where pushing helps us.

notes.title: SOP-05 · Escalation
notes.body:
What you hand to Logan instead of answering. Handing something over is never the wrong call.

## Escalate the same day, by text

- **A high-value prospect** — team lead, 25+ deals, multiple crews or trucks, more than one location, already running ads. Never work these yourself. Logan and Garrett take them.
- Any question about **contracts, refunds, guarantees, cancellation, or anything legal**.
- Anyone asking about **the CRM, the automation packages, or anything priced per person**. You never put a number on those.
- **Any request for a discount** — however small, however close they sound to saying yes.
- Someone who says they are **already a client**, or who has a complaint about us.
- **An angry call**, or anyone who asks not to be contacted again.
- Anything you would otherwise have to guess at.

## How to escalate without losing the call

> "That is a fair question, and I would rather get you the right answer than guess at it. Let me put Logan on it — can I grab you ten minutes with him?"

This makes you look better, not worse. A rep who says "I do not know, let me get you someone who does" reads as honest. A rep who guesses reads as a salesman, and they hear it instantly.

## What you do not escalate

Normal objections. "What is it cost," "I already have a website," "just send me the link," "not interested" — those are yours, they are in the objections module, and handling them is the job.

Escalation is for things outside your authority, not things that are hard.

## What to expect back

Logan answers within the business day. Do not hold a live call waiting on him — book the appointment, escalate after, and let him sort it before the call happens.

notes.title: SOP-06 · How you get paid
notes.body:
One way you earn today, and what is likely coming. No invoices to submit, no forms to chase.

## Before your first payment

- Signed representative agreement
- Completed W-9
- Payment method on file

You are an independent contractor. Nothing is withheld from what you are paid, and you will get a 1099-NEC after year end if you earn more than the IRS threshold. What you owe in tax on it is yours to handle — worth setting some aside from the first payment rather than the last.

## Commission — 25% of the build

- **25% of the collected build fee** on every deal you sourced. Nothing is taken off the top first — it is 25% of what the client actually paid for the build.
- The build runs $749 to $1,549 depending on size and how much automation goes behind it, so that is roughly **$187 to $387 a deal**.
- The monthly is **not** commissionable, and neither are the CRM or automation packages — those are priced per person and quoted by Logan.
- Paid on the **5th of the month** after the client's money clears.

## The three states

- **Pending** — the deal closed. Your commission is counted and visible, but it is not money yet.
- **Earned** — the client actually paid. This is the real state and it is what gets paid out.
- **Voided** — the client cancelled or never paid. It leaves your totals.

Commission follows collected money, not signed paper. A client who signs and never pays is not a deal, and we are not going to pretend otherwise in either direction — the day they pay, it is yours.

## What this does not include yet

Right now you are paid on closed deals only. There is no payment for booking an appointment that does not convert.

We expect to add something on held appointments once there is enough volume to price it properly. When that happens you will get it in writing before it starts, and it will be in addition to the 25%, not instead of it.

! **Until you see it in writing, assume it does not exist.**

## What you submit

Nothing. Logan reconciles commission against what actually landed in the bank, and you will get a short statement with each payment showing which deals it covers.

## If something looks wrong

Raise it within thirty days of the payment and we will go through it together against the log. That is why SOP-02 exists — an honest log is the thing that protects you here, not us.

## Your costs

You cover your own phone, internet and wherever you work from. You set your own hours, you use your own equipment, and you are free to work with other companies while you work with us.
